intro: Castle Howard is the great country house in the Howardian Hills of North Yorkshire, begun in 1699, about fifteen miles north-east of York. You do not need a ticket to meet two of its oaks: they stand in the visitor car park, a minute's walk apart. One has lost its top and grown a new crown from a single limb; the other twists into a knot of branches. A reader sent us both.
meta_description: Two old oaks a reader found in the visitor car park at Castle Howard, North Yorkshire: one with a broken top, one twisting. Where they stand.
question_meta: Two old oaks in the Castle Howard car park, North Yorkshire, sent by a reader: where they stand and how to tell them apart.
question_answer: Two old oaks stand in the visitor car park at Castle Howard, near Malton in North Yorkshire, about sixty metres apart: the Broken Oak by the footpath and the Twisting Oak among the parked cars. Both are outside the paid house and gardens.
question_context: A reader visiting Castle Howard in November 2026 photographed two oaks in its visitor car park and sent them to us. The first stands on the grass between a footpath and the car park rail. Its trunk is a broad, deeply fluted column whose top broke off long ago, leaving a jagged stump, and below the break one great limb has grown out sideways into a whole new crown. The second stands about sixty metres away among the parked cars, behind a low wooden rail and a patch of rough grass. Its trunk is short and massive, ivy climbs one side, and its limbs bend, double back and cross one another into a knotted crown, with cut stubs where branches have been removed. Neither tree has a measured girth, a sourced age or a name that we know of, and we have not yet confirmed which oak species they are. The house itself was begun in 1699, but that does not date the trees. Both can be seen without a ticket for the house and gardens. If you know either tree's story or have measured it, tell us on its page.

faq.q: Are there old trees at Castle Howard you can see for free?
faq.a: Yes. Two old oaks stand in the visitor car park, outside the paid house and gardens, about sixty metres apart.

faq.q: How do I find the oaks in the Castle Howard car park?
faq.a: The Broken Oak stands on the grass by the footpath at the edge of the car park, its top snapped off. The Twisting Oak stands among the parked cars behind a low wooden rail.

faq.q: How old are the Castle Howard car park oaks?
faq.a: We do not know yet. Neither has a sourced age or girth; if you have measured one, tell us on its page.

trees.story:
Most people who come to Castle Howard walk straight past this oak on their way from the car to the house. A reader stopped, and sent us its photograph from the path beside it.

It is worth the pause. The trunk rises as a great grey column, broad at the foot and deeply fluted, and then simply stops. The top broke off long ago and left a jagged stump standing above everything else. The tree carried on regardless. From just below the break one huge limb turned outwards and grew a whole new crown, and in the reader's November photograph its branches spread far over the grass and the car park rail, still holding a few brown leaves. Across the parking, more old oaks stand in the same rough grass.

We do not know its girth, its age, or whether the estate has a name for it. The house behind it was begun in 1699, but that tells us nothing certain about the tree. If you know its story, or have put a tape round it, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Walk round to the path side to see how the broken column and the new crown fit together.

trees.access: In the visitor car park at Castle Howard, outside the paid house and gardens. We have not confirmed whether parking is charged.
trees.story:
In the car park at Castle Howard, among the hatchbacks and estate cars, stands an oak that looks as if it stopped halfway through a dance. A reader photographed it there in November and sent it to us.

The trunk is short and massive, with ivy climbing one side, and from it the limbs go every way but straight. They bend, double back, cross over one another and twist upwards again, so that the crown is a knot of dark elbows against the grey sky. Cut stubs along the branches show where limbs have been taken off over the years. A low wooden rail and a patch of rough grass keep the cars a few steps from its foot, and behind it a line of tall old trees runs off towards the open park.

We have no girth, no age and no name for it yet. If you have measured it, or know what the estate calls it, tell us here and we will add it with your figures.

Stand on the grass side, away from the cars, and follow one limb with your eye from the trunk to its tip. A second big oak, its top long broken, stands a minute's walk away by the footpath.
